lead: Modular arithmetic keeps only the remainder after division by a fixed positive integer n. Two integers with the same remainder are called congruent. This turns the infinite integers into n residue classes, a finite set written Z<sub>n</sub>. The Chinese remainder theorem goes the other way: several congruences with coprime moduli combine into one congruence modulo their product. These ideas appear in clock arithmetic, check digits, hash tables, and in the arithmetic behind UPI references and digital signatures.
prereq: You need: 4.6 Divisibility, primes, GCD and Euclidean algorithm for gcd and the extended Euclidean method, and equivalence classes from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Fix a positive integer n, called the modulus. We say a ≡ b (mod n) when n divides a − b. For example, 23 ≡ 2 (mod 3), because 3 divides 21. The remainder of a on division by n is the unique r with 0 ≤ r < n and a ≡ r (mod n).

blocks.where: a and b are integers; n is the positive modulus; | means divides.

blocks.text: The residue class of a modulo n is [a]<sub>n</sub> = {a + kn : k ∈ Z}. There are exactly n classes, [0]<sub>n</sub> through [n−1]<sub>n</sub>. Their set is Z<sub>n</sub>. Addition and multiplication on classes are defined by [a]+[b]=[a+b] and [a][b]=[ab]. These operations are well defined: changing a or b by a multiple of n changes the answer by a multiple of n. For example, in Z<sub>12</sub>, [10]+[5]=[15]=[3], which is clock arithmetic: 10 o'clock plus 5 hours is 3 o'clock.

Under addition, Zn is a cyclic group of order n (see 4.3). Under multiplication it is not a group: [0] has no inverse, and [2] has no inverse modulo 4. The invertible classes are those [a] with gcd(a,n)=1.

A linear congruence has the form ax ≡ b (mod n). Here a and b are integers and x is the unknown class modulo n. Let d = gcd(a,n). The congruence has a solution if and only if d divides b. When it has solutions, there are exactly d different solutions modulo n.

Case d=1. Then a has an inverse modulo n: a number a<sup>−1</sup> with aa<sup>−1</sup> ≡ 1 (mod n). Multiply both sides by a<sup>−1</sup> to get the unique solution x ≡ a<sup>−1</sup>b (mod n). The extended Euclidean algorithm finds this inverse. Run it on a and n to get integers s,t with as + nt = 1. Then s ≡ a<sup>−1</sup> (mod n). For example, 3x ≡ 1 (mod 7). The algorithm gives 3·5 + 7·(−2) = 1, so 3<sup>−1</sup> ≡ 5 (mod 7). Then 3x ≡ 2 (mod 7) has x ≡ 5·2 = 10 ≡ 3 (mod 7).

Case d>1 and d divides b. Divide the congruence and the modulus by d: (a/d)x ≡ (b/d) (mod n/d). Now gcd(a/d,n/d)=1, so solve as above. The single solution modulo n/d gives d solutions modulo n, namely x<sub>0</sub>, x<sub>0</sub> + n/d, ..., x<sub>0</sub> + (d−1)n/d. Example: 6x ≡ 4 (mod 8). Here d=2, and 2 divides 4. Divide by 2: 3x ≡ 2 (mod 4). Since 3<sup>−1</sup> ≡ 3 (mod 4), x ≡ 6 ≡ 2 (mod 4). Modulo 8 the solutions are x ≡ 2 and x ≡ 6.

sections.h3: Chinese remainder theorem and number-theory theorems

blocks.text: The Chinese remainder theorem (CRT) solves simultaneous congruences. Let n<sub>1</sub>, n<sub>2</sub>, ..., n<sub>k</sub> be positive integers that are pairwise coprime: gcd(n<sub>i</sub>,n<sub>j</sub>)=1 for i≠j. Let N=n<sub>1</sub>n<sub>2</sub>...n<sub>k</sub>. The system x ≡ a<sub>1</sub> (mod n<sub>1</sub>), ..., x ≡ a<sub>k</sub> (mod n<sub>k</sub>) has exactly one solution modulo N. If the moduli are not pairwise coprime, the theorem does not apply directly; the system may have no solution or a solution modulo a smaller number, depending on compatibility.

To solve by hand, combine two congruences at a time. Write the first as x = a<sub>1</sub> + n<sub>1</sub>t. Put it into the second, solve for t modulo n<sub>2</sub>, and substitute back. The result is one congruence modulo n<sub>1</sub>n<sub>2</sub>. Repeat with the next congruence. The worked example below uses this method.
Euler's totient φ(n) counts the integers k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n and gcd(k,n)=1. For a prime p, φ(p)=p−1. For distinct primes p,q, φ(pq)=(p−1)(q−1). For example, φ(10)=4, counting 1,3,7,9.
Wilson's theorem: if p is prime, then (p−1)! ≡ −1 (mod p). For p=5, 4! = 24 ≡ 4 ≡ −1 (mod 5).

Euler's totient theorem: if gcd(a,n)=1, then a<sup>φ(n)</sup> ≡ 1 (mod n). Fermat's little theorem is the prime case: if p is prime and p does not divide a, then a<sup>p−1</sup> ≡ 1 (mod p). For example, φ(10)=4 and 3<sup>4</sup>=81≡1 (mod 10); and modulo 7, 2<sup>6</sup>=64≡1 (mod 7).

figure.caption: Three congruences with coprime moduli 3, 5 and 7 combine into x ≡ 23 (mod 105). Reducing 23 modulo each modulus recovers 2, 3 and 2.

spec.title: Chinese remainder theorem example
spec.aria: Three congruences modulo 3, 5 and 7 combine to the single congruence x ≡ 23 modulo 105, which is checked by reducing 23.

examples.question: Solve the system x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5), x ≡ 2 (mod 7). Give the general solution and the least non-negative solution.
steps: Combine the first two congruences. Write x = 2 + 3t with t an integer.
The inverse of 3 modulo 5 is 2, because 3·2 = 6 ≡ 1 (mod 5). So t ≡ 2 (mod 5).
Write t = 2 + 5s. Then x = 2 + 3(2 + 5s) = 8 + 15s. Thus x ≡ 8 (mod 15).
Reduce modulo 7: 8 ≡ 1 and 15 ≡ 1, so 1 + s ≡ 2 (mod 7). Hence s ≡ 1 (mod 7).
The general solution is x ≡ 23 (mod 105). The least non-negative solution is 23.
examples.answer: The solution is x ≡ 23 (mod 105); the least non-negative solution is 23.

traps: Do not apply the Chinese remainder theorem unless the moduli are pairwise coprime. If they are not, check compatibility first. For example, x ≡ 1 (mod 4) and x ≡ 2 (mod 6) has no solution because modulo 2 it demands x odd and x even.
A congruence ax ≡ b (mod n) may have solutions even when gcd(a,n) ≠ 1. It is solvable exactly when gcd(a,n) divides b; do not declare it impossible just because a has no inverse.
When gcd(a,n)=d divides b, the number of solutions modulo n is d, not 1. After dividing by d, the modulus becomes n/d, and then you lift back to d classes modulo n.
Fermat's little theorem needs a prime modulus p and p not dividing a. Euler's theorem needs gcd(a,n)=1. Applying either without its condition gives wrong answers.
An inverse from the extended Euclidean algorithm may be negative. Reduce it modulo n to the range 0 to n−1 before using it in the final answer.

quiz.a: a ≡ b (mod n) means n divides a − b, where n is a positive integer.

quiz.q: Why is addition in Z<sub>n</sub> well defined?
quiz.a: If a′ ≡ a (mod n) and b′ ≡ b (mod n), then a′+b′ ≡ a+b (mod n). So the class [a+b] does not depend on which representatives are chosen.
The inverse of 5 modulo 11 is 9, because 5·9=45≡1 (mod 11). Then x ≡ 9·3=27≡5 (mod 11). Answer: x ≡ 5 (mod 11).
gcd(6,8)=2, and 2 divides 4. Divide by 2: 3x ≡ 2 (mod 4). The inverse of 3 modulo 4 is 3, so x ≡ 3·2=6≡2 (mod 4). Modulo 8 the solutions are x ≡ 2 and x ≡ 6.

quiz.q: Does the Chinese remainder theorem apply directly to x ≡ 1 (mod 4) and x ≡ 3 (mod 6)? Solve the system.
quiz.a: No, gcd(4,6)=2, so the moduli are not coprime. The system is compatible. Write x=1+4t. Then 1+4t≡3 (mod 6), so 4t≡2 (mod 6). Divide by 2: 2t≡1 (mod 3), so t≡2 (mod 3). Then x=1+4(2+3s)=9+12s. Answer: x ≡ 9 (mod 12).

quiz.q: Compute φ(12) and verify Euler's totient theorem for a=5 and n=12.
quiz.a: The numbers 1,5,7,11 are coprime to 12, so φ(12)=4. Also 5<sup>4</sup>=625, and 625−1=624 is divisible by 12. Hence 5<sup>4</sup> ≡ 1 (mod 12).

quiz.q: Solve x ≡ 1 (mod 5) and x ≡ 2 (mod 7) using the Chinese remainder theorem.
quiz.a: Write x=1+5t. Then 1+5t≡2 (mod 7), so 5t≡1 (mod 7). The inverse of 5 modulo 7 is 3, so t≡3 (mod 7). Then x=1+5(3+7s)=16+35s. Answer: x ≡ 16 (mod 35).
Here (p−1)! = 6! = 720. Since 720 = 7·102 + 6, we get 720 ≡ 6 ≡ −1 (mod 7). Wilson's theorem holds.

beyond: Not for the exam. The Chinese remainder theorem is used to speed up big-integer arithmetic by splitting numbers into residues modulo several coprime primes. RSA and other public-key systems rely on modular exponentiation, Euler's theorem and modular inverses. Hash tables and error-detecting codes use remainders and congruence checks. Search next for RSA, modular exponentiation, and CRT-based secret sharing.
